recordings.text: Interesting move: one piece lands where it touches several targets, and the reply can't comfortably cover them all. Worth replaying to see how it got there.
Here's an experiment worth running: which enemy piece could now jump to a square that hits several targets? After this move, a fork like that is on the table.
Set the other candidate beside this one, and a fork appears in it, a lone attacker aimed at several targets. This move takes the game down a different road.
Pinned against its own king, that piece is stuck. Ask what it would like to do next; leaving its line isn't one of its legal options.
What happens to the piece in front of the king now? After this move, it can be pinned there, and a pinned piece against the king can't legally step off that line.
Compare the stronger candidate: it pins an enemy piece to its king. With this move, that piece stays free to wander.
Here's the skewer idea in action. The front piece is forced aside, and that exposes whatever stood behind it on the line.
Run the other side's best reply forward: a skewer appears, driving the front piece away and leaving whatever stood behind it open.
There was a skewer hiding in the other candidate. Hit the front piece, and the one behind becomes the real target. That idea wasn't tried here.
Follow the logic: take the defender first, and the piece it was looking after is suddenly on its own.
One question to keep asking: which pieces are defenders, and what happens if they're captured? After this move, one of them can be taken.
The stronger candidate removes a defender, and the piece it protected becomes vulnerable. Worth comparing the two moves side by side.
Here's the back-rank theme to test: the king's own pieces stand where its escape squares should be, and that last rank becomes the target.
Where could the king run if a heavy piece arrived on its last rank? After this move, nowhere, and a back-rank mate is available to the other side.
The stronger candidate had a back-rank mate in it, with the enemy king boxed in by its own pieces. A pattern worth testing on the board.
One step nearer promotion for the pawn. Count the steps left and the pieces that can still stop it; that comparison tells the story.
What can stop that enemy pawn now? After this move, it has a clearer route toward promotion, so the race deserves attention.
The other candidate pushes a pawn toward promotion, while this one leaves it waiting. Compare how the race looks in each case.
Watch the line open up: the front piece moves, and the piece standing behind it suddenly has a target.
Look for pieces lined up behind each other on the other side. After this move, one of them can step aside and release a discovered attack.
The other candidate holds a discovered attack, a front piece stepping off the line to release the one behind. This move doesn't open that line.
One option, and suddenly there are threats in two directions. Try every defense against it; one reply rarely handles both.
After this move, can one enemy move make two threats at once? The search says yes, so a double attack is available to the other side.
Set the stronger candidate beside this move: it creates two threats at once, while this move creates no such pair.
A deflection. The defender gets pulled toward a new job, and the duty it was doing is left undone.
What is each defender responsible for here? After this move, one can be lured away from that task.
The other candidate would have drawn a defender away from its duty. Try it on the board and see what falls apart behind it.
That piece had nobody looking after it, and now it's captured. A simple idea, and a good habit to keep testing for.
An unprotected piece was available to capture with the other candidate. Before quiet moves, it's worth a quick sweep for loose pieces.
Which defender used to cover that piece? After this move nothing protects it, so it's free for the other side to collect.
What was this piece guarding before it moved? It was the only real defender of another piece, which is now open to capture.
What did the opponent's last move change? It created a threat, and this reply doesn't respond to it, so a piece is still open to capture.
Follow the exchange one move further. The recapture takes something more valuable than what was won, so the trade comes out behind.
Out comes a minor piece from its starting square, ready to take part in the plans.
Another candidate develops a minor piece off its starting square. Worth comparing the two setups.
The rook steps onto a file where neither side has a pawn. Where could it go from here?
One candidate puts a rook on a fully open file. Set it beside this move and compare the activity.
This move parks the rook on a semi-open file, clear of its own pawns, with at least one enemy pawn further along.
A different move places a rook on a semi-open file, where its own pawns are gone but enemy pawns still stand.
Now there's a passed pawn worth following. No enemy pawn, on its own file or either neighbor, can block or capture it on the way.
Another candidate creates a passed pawn, one that no enemy pawn can stop on its own file or either adjacent one.
The passed pawn is a square closer to the end of its run. How many are left, and who can stop it?
Another candidate pushes the passed pawn further. This one leaves it where it is.
This creates an isolated pawn, with no pawn of its color on the files next door.
Another candidate would have isolated a pawn, leaving its adjacent files without friendly pawns.
A piece that had no protection picks up a defender here.
One alternative gives a defender to a piece that's currently unprotected.
After this move, a certain piece has nobody defending it. Keep watching that weakness; on its own, it doesn't mean the piece can be won.
Another candidate would have taken away a piece's last defender, which by itself wouldn't settle whether it could be won.
With this move the king has a fresh square to escape to. So which piece got out of the way?
Another candidate would have given the king one more legal square. Try to spot which piece would have moved out of the way.
Castling. The king travels two squares, and its rook jumps to the inner side of it.
Castling was among the ideas, moving king and rook in one turn.
With this capture the bishop pair is split, so that side's remaining bishop covers just one square color.
Another candidate captures a bishop and breaks up the opposing pair.
Doubled pawns: after this move, two pawns of one color stack up on a single file.
Another candidate leads to doubled pawns, two of one color stacked on a file.
Forced checkmate now sits in the other side's hands. Let's trace the attack back and find where the defense could have changed.
A forced checkmate was available with another candidate, and this move doesn't play it. It's worth setting up that line and walking through it.
A sacrifice that passes the test. What if the material is taken? The line that was checked says the idea still stands.
Line up the candidates, and only one keeps things playable. All the other options that were examined end up losing.
Of all the candidates examined, this was the one that kept the advantage alive; every other one ends up losing.
What's the first thing the other side can do here? Capture something, straight away. That's the reply to look at before any other.
What does the strongest reply look like? It's a check, so king safety comes before anything else in the comparison.
The engine has another candidate it prefers. Play both against the strongest reply and see where they part ways.
Compared with the engine's top candidate, this one gives up some value. Follow the reply, and the gap between them becomes visible.
This candidate holds up well beside the engine's choices; hardly anything is conceded.
A workable idea. The engine prefers another move, but most of the position's value is still here.
The human-move model rates this a natural move, and it's easy to see why. The engine prefers another candidate, and the reply reveals the price of this one.
The human-move model doesn't expect this candidate, but the engine's test says strong. An unusual idea that holds up.
Just one option held the position here, and the human-move model thinks few players would find that defense. It's a good one to set up and explore.
An idea few would find, going by the human-move model and the searched alternatives. It's worth revisiting more than once.
This kept the position together, and judging by the human-move model and the searched alternatives, few players would have come up with it. Good exploring.
Here the move most players reach for is also the strongest: the human-move model expects it, and the engine's comparison finds nothing that beats it.
The human-move model rates this natural, and the engine finds it strong, though its own preference is a different move.
The clock was nearly empty for this one.
This came quickly, with a comfortable amount of time still on the clock.
This move came after a long think, at the clock's expense.
This move fits into a recognized opening.
Here the known theory runs out. From now on, it's open territory to explore.
After the earlier error, this brings the position back to playable. A useful turnaround to compare with what came before.
Playable once more after the earlier error, and mistakes from the other side helped make that possible.
The opponent's last move gave something away, and this candidate uses it. Compare it with the quieter options to see what it gains.
The opponent's last move gave something away, and this reply lets it go. There was a stronger answer to try instead.
This same issue already showed up once in this game. Put the two moments side by side, and the pattern gets easier to recognize.
Earlier this piece lost its protection; now it's covered again. Compare the two positions and see what changed.
Several small concessions have added up, and this move is yet another. None of them is big alone; together they make a real difference.
From that point to the recorded win, the advantage held. Following how it was carried through is a good study.
Several other saved games share this exact issue. Comparing them side by side could reveal a pattern worth working on.
Checkmate. The king is out of escapes, and that settles the game.
Checkmate; there's no legal move left for the defending king. The interesting question now is where the defense could have gone differently.
A draw. The result is settled, though the earlier choices are still open for exploring.
Look over the position, pick a candidate, and test it when you're ready.
Different candidate needed. Try another idea and compare the replies.
That attempt didn't produce any result. Submit the same option again.
According to the saved engine analysis, whoever played this move can force checkmate.
A forced mate, the saved engine analysis says, now belongs to the opponent of whoever played this move.
Tally it up after the saved line, and the side that played this move has more material.
Tally it up after the saved line, and the side that played this move has less material.
This move is accepted by the exercise, though the moves shown don't reveal a clear tactical reason, and it's better not to make one up.
Not this move, according to the exercise, and nothing in the moves shown makes a clear tactical case. Try another one.
That matches one of the saved answers, and in this exercise the saved answers decide.
That move isn't among the exercise's saved answers, though another legal move can still be good chess.
Look again at the move and the idea that drives it, and then head to the next position.
Nice choice. The idea behind it is what carries over to the next position, so keep that close.
Practice saved; the review schedule hasn't moved.
Solved. This recall keeps its relearning status for the time being.
This is the starting point, before any of the moves in this line.
Next move. What does it change?
Check. Before anything else, the king has to be dealt with.
Out of check, the king is safe from it now.
Promotion: having crossed the board, the pawn trades itself in for a new piece.
Promotion, and the fresh piece checks the king at once.
Promoting the pawn ends the game in checkmate.
Promoting the pawn is also how its own king escapes check.
One piece is captured and leaves the board.
A capture, and the capturing piece gives check.
One capture, and it ends in checkmate.
Taking a piece is also how the king gets out of check here.
A capture onto the last rank, followed by promotion.
The pawn captures, promotes, and the new piece checks at once.
A pawn capture, a promotion, and checkmate, all in one move.
Capturing and promoting at once, the pawn also takes its own king out of check.
Castling, with check as a bonus.
Castling delivers checkmate here.
Here's the fork working: a single attacker threatens several targets and then picks one of them off. In this example, there's a net material gain as well.
Why can't this piece make the marked capture? Its king stands behind it, and leaving the line would expose that king.
The attacked piece is pinned to its king, so its only legal moves are the ones that keep the king covered.
Why does nobody recapture? The defenders are all pinned, each one shielding its king. That's what makes the capture work, and the line shown finishes ahead on material.
Follow the pinned piece: the king behind it keeps it stuck on the line, and it gets captured before the sequence is done.
When the front piece steps out of the way, whatever it was shielding is captured.
The king is checked off the line, and the same attacker then collects what stood behind it.
Capture the only defender first, and the piece it was protecting is next. One capture opens the way for the other.
Once the defender is pulled off its post, the piece it was minding gets captured.
Move the blocker, and the piece behind it captures along the line that just opened.
When the piece steps off the line, the line behind it gives check.
Double check: two pieces give check at the same time, and only a king move can answer it.
One target is hit by the moving piece, another by the line it opens. In this case, it's the piece behind that collects.
The pawn promotes, and by the end of this example that side is also ahead on material overall.
The captured piece had no protection, and the side that took it ends this example ahead on material.
The attacking piece had been held by a relative pin, until the opponent's previous move let it go. Freed, it captures a target that stayed put, in the line shown.
The marked reply is among the other side's legal candidates. Test it on the board and watch the position change.
Before choosing a move, ask whether any piece could be captured without a decent recapture.
Before a quiet option, check whether any enemy piece is sitting there unprotected.
Among the forcing ideas, is there one piece that could reach two valuable targets at once?
When a piece is pinned, what's behind it, the king or a piece worth more? That decides how much it can move.
Is anything lined up behind the first target? Sometimes something more valuable is waiting on the same line.
Before a defender gets traded off, list the pieces it protects.
When a piece steps off a line, ask what that line can reach now.
Search for one move that makes two threats, counting checks and lines that open up.
Before a back-rank defender moves, does the king still have a square to escape to?
How many squares does that pawn need to promote, and which of its moves would need an answer?
Before a defender moves, check which pieces were relying on it.
Before capturing, weigh what you gain against what the recapture would take back.
Is there a forcing exchange that could pull a defender off a second job?
This exercise measures options against its saved answers, though a legal move outside them can still be good chess.
The line shown uses strong replies, which aren't necessarily the only possible ones.
Material changes are measured inside the line shown, starting from its own first position. For the piece values behind them, check the written explanation.
A simple tactical reason doesn't show up in the saved line, and there's no need to guess a positional one. Walk through it and test each reply as a candidate.
How the explanation works depends on the answer policy saved with this exercise; the written notes record which setting applies.

The record marks this attempt as revealed, and the solution waits below.
Solved, after one retry or more. The earlier miss stays in the record next to the solution.
Every move correct, all the way to the solution.
This puzzle wants a different option, though the correct moves you played earlier are still saved.

Look carefully, compare candidates, and move when the line is clear.
There isn't enough engine analysis to explain this position, so no guessing here.
Review paused for a bit. Carry on below, or test a candidate on the board.
Pick a move to revisit, or test a candidate of your own on the board.

This move is borrowed from a known opening.

We're still exploring the book's territory.
Another position the book has an entry for.

The known line keeps unfolding.
One more idea the book already knows.
There's still more book to explore here.
Book, once again.
A move the book already lists. The book tells us where we are, not which option is strongest.
The human-move model rates this natural, and it's easy to see the appeal, but after it the other side has a forced checkmate. Let's trace back where the defense could have changed.
Another candidate forced checkmate. This one, a natural idea in the human-move model's eyes, lets that chance pass. When the enemy king looks exposed, test the forcing moves first.
A natural move, as the human-move model sees it, but it allows an immediate capture. What can the other side take right away? That's the first question.
The human-move model rates this natural, and the engine has a candidate it prefers. Compare the two against the reply, and the cost of this one shows up.
Natural, by the human-move model, yet it lets an enemy piece fork several targets. Which piece could make that jump? Find it first.
The human-move model rates this natural, but now a skewer is open to the other side, which can drive off the front piece and expose what's behind.
Every other candidate in the search loses, and this one keeps the position playable. The human-move model thinks few players would find that defense. A great resource to have discovered.
Of all the candidates examined, only this keeps the game playable. The engine's top option, and one the human-move model and the searched alternatives say is hard to find. Nicely spotted.
The advantage survives through this move and no other, while every other examined option loses, and the human-move model rates it a hard resource to find. Really well spotted.
Keeping the advantage took exactly this move; the others lose. Hard to find by the human-move model's measure, and the winner of the engine's comparison. A real discovery.
A fork, a lone piece eyeing several targets at once. Not a move the human-move model expects, and yet the engine's test says strong. Unusual ideas deserve a look.
A well-hidden fork, one piece reaching several targets. The human-move model and the searched alternatives call this move difficult, and the engine puts it first.
The pinned piece sits in front of its king and can't legally step off its line. The human-move model gives this move a low chance of being played, while the engine's comparison finds it strong.
A king pin, freezing a piece where it stands. A well-hidden move that the engine ranks first and the human-move model rarely sees coming.
The human-move model rates it natural, but this piece was the only real defender of another one, which is now open to capture.
The only defender walks off, and the piece it was covering is now capturable. Just one of the searched moves would have held, a defense the human-move model expects few players to find.
The opponent's last move created a threat to test against, and this reply, a natural candidate in the human-move model's eyes, doesn't answer it. One piece can still be captured.
The threat set up by the opponent's last move stands, and a piece can still be captured. The holding option was a different move, and the human-move model counts that defense difficult to spot.
The human-move model rates this capture natural, but follow it one more move: the recapture takes something more valuable.
This capture runs into a more valuable recapture. Of the searched moves, only one kept things together, and the human-move model rates it as easy to overlook.
A fork: one piece lands where it hits several targets. Here instinct and search agree, since the human-move model's favorite pick is also the move at the top of the engine's list.
One piece now threatens several targets together. Natural in the human-move model's eyes and strong in the engine's test, though the engine's own choice is a different one.
After this move, the other side has a fork available. Only a single idea held among those searched, and by the human-move model it's a tough one to find.
The other candidate had a fork in it. This move, a natural option in the human-move model's eyes, takes a different path.
The defense that held came with a fork, and it went untried. By the human-move model's estimate, few players would land on it.

A pin: the piece shielding its king can't legally step off the line. Instinct and search land on the same option this time, since the human-move model expects it and nothing in the engine's comparison tops it.
A piece gets pinned against its king. As ideas go, it's the natural one for the human-move model and a strong one for the engine, which would pick something else.
Natural, by the human-move model, but now a piece can be pinned against its king and lose the freedom to leave its line.
A pin against the king is now within the other side's reach. The move that held was elsewhere, and in the human-move model's view few would find it, so it's worth setting up and exploring.
The other candidate pins an enemy piece to its king. This one, natural for the human-move model, leaves that piece free.
The defense that held pinned a piece to its king, and it went untried. The human-move model gives that defense a low chance of being found.
A skewer: push the front piece aside, and whatever stood behind it is there for the taking. Top of the engine's option list, and the human-move model says few would find it. Worth remembering.
An unexpected skewer that drives the front piece off its line. Seldom a human-move model candidate, and the engine's test passes it as strong.
Chase the front piece away, and what stood behind it is exposed. If we line up every option, the human-move model's favorite is also the engine's, which is a nice thing to discover.
A skewer, lined up along one line. Natural as the human-move model scores it and strong as the engine tests it, with the engine's favorite being another move.
A skewer has just become possible for the other side. A single searched defense survived, one the human-move model rates as difficult.
The other candidate had a skewer. This one, a natural idea in the human-move model's eyes, leaves that line alone.
The defense that held used a skewer, and it went untried. By the human-move model, it's a defense that rarely gets found.
The defender is captured, and its protection disappears. Difficult to spot, as the human-move model scores it, and the best idea the engine found. Good exploring.
A defender is taken, leaving the piece it covered exposed. Few players would try it, by the human-move model's estimate, yet it passes the engine's test as strong.
Take the defender, and the piece it protected is on its own. Natural by the human-move model's lights, and the winner of the engine's comparison too.
This captures a defender. Put the two views together: the human-move model expects it, and the engine likes it while choosing a different move.
The human-move model rates this natural, but one defender becomes capturable, leaving the piece it covers unprotected.
After this move, one defender can be taken. Just one of the searched moves would have held, a defense the human-move model expects few players to find.
The other candidate takes a defender off the board. This one, a natural option in the human-move model's eyes, leaves it on duty.
The defense that held captured a defender, and it went untried. The human-move model expects most players to overlook it.
A back-rank theme: no exit squares remain, thanks to the king's own pieces. The human-move model gives this move a low chance of being found, with the engine choosing it ahead of everything else.
A back-rank theme, with the king stuck on its last rank. Surprising to the human-move model yet sturdy under the engine's test, a reminder to keep unusual candidates on the list.
The back rank is the weak spot, and the king can't get off it. The move a player reaches for first, by the human-move model, also survives every engine test as the best.
On the back rank, a mating idea is taking shape. A sturdy option. Natural by the human-move model, strong by the engine, whose preference lies with another idea.
A pawn moves toward promotion. Count the steps, and the race becomes clear. The engine prefers this move to every other, and the human-move model and searched alternatives say it's hard to see.
An unexpected pawn push toward the last rank. The human-move model wouldn't predict this move, while the engine's comparison comes back strong.
A pawn gets one step closer to promotion. Test it two ways and the answers match, natural for the human-move model and unbeaten in the engine's comparison.
This move nudges a pawn closer to queening. The human-move model sees an everyday, natural idea; the engine sees a strong one, though its own choice differs.
Natural, by the human-move model, but an enemy pawn now has a clearer path to promotion. How many steps does it need?
One of the enemy pawns has a free run toward promotion now. The holding option was a different move, and the human-move model counts that defense difficult to spot.
The other candidate pushes a pawn toward promotion. This one, natural for the human-move model, keeps it waiting.
The defense that held advanced a pawn toward promotion, and it went untried. The human-move model thinks few players would find it.

The front piece clears the way, and the one behind it gets its chance to attack. Best in the engine's comparison and tricky in the human-move model's estimate, which is exactly what makes the find special.
A discovered attack, from an angle few would try. Unexpected by the human-move model's standards, strong when the engine tests it.
The line opens, and the piece hiding behind joins the attack. Here's a case where the human-move model's expectation and the engine's preference point at one idea.
A discovered attack opens up the line. Weighing both views, it's natural for the human-move model and strong for the engine, which leans toward another idea.
The human-move model rates this natural, yet a discovered attack becomes possible: an enemy piece can step aside and unleash the one behind it.
The other side can now unmask a discovered attack. Of the searched moves, only one kept things together, and the human-move model rates it as easy to overlook.
The other candidate releases a discovered attack along the line. This one, a natural move in the human-move model's eyes, keeps that line shut.
The defense that held opened a line for a discovered attack, and it went untried. As the human-move model sees things, few would spot it.
One option, two threats. Not an obvious idea for the human-move model, and the engine's favorite. Well found.
An unexpected idea that makes two threats together. This isn't where the human-move model looks first, and still the engine's test comes back strong.
Two targets come under fire from one move. As moves go, this is both the expected one, by the human-move model, and the top one, by the engine.
A double attack, two threats needing two answers. Natural to the human-move model and solid under the engine's test, even if the engine would play something different.
Natural, by the human-move model, but now one enemy move can make two threats at once.
The other side now has a move that makes two threats. Only a single idea held among those searched, and by the human-move model it's a tough one to find.
The other candidate made two threats at once. This one, natural for the human-move model, doesn't create that pair.
The defense that held made two threats at once, and it went untried. By the human-move model's estimate, few players would land on it.
A deflection, coaxing the defender off its duty. The engine's top option, and one the human-move model and the searched alternatives say is hard to find. Nicely spotted.
The defender gets coaxed away by an unexpected move. An unlikely pick in the human-move model's eyes, and in the engine's comparison a strong one, so the imagination paid off.
Lure the defender somewhere else, and its old post is left uncovered. Two different tests, one winner: natural in the human-move model, first among the engine's choices.
A deflection of a defender. This is a move the human-move model would anticipate, and the engine rates it strong while keeping a different one as its pick.
The human-move model rates this natural, but one defender can now be lured away, leaving what it guards uncovered.
A defender can now be lured off its task. The move that held was elsewhere, and in the human-move model's view few would find it, so it's worth setting up and exploring.
The other candidate deflects a defender. This one, a natural option in the human-move model's eyes, leaves it at its post.
The defense that held deflected a defender, and it went untried. The human-move model gives that defense a low chance of being found.
A piece nobody was guarding is picked off. Hard to find by the human-move model's measure, and the winner of the engine's comparison. A real discovery.
A loose piece collected by an unexpected idea. The human-move model calls it improbable, while the engine's test comes back strong, and that gap is the interesting part to explore.
Nobody was guarding that piece, so this move simply collects it. The intuitive option wins the comparison outright, natural to the human-move model and best in the engine's search.
This picks up an undefended piece. Easy to reach for, says the human-move model, and strong, says the engine, which picks a different option itself.
The other candidate captures an unprotected piece. This one, natural for the human-move model, leaves it on the board.
The defense that held captured an unprotected piece, and it went untried. By the human-move model, it's a defense that rarely gets found.
The human-move model rates this natural, but it leaves a piece without protection for the other side to take.
A piece is left with no protection at all. A single searched defense survived, one the human-move model rates as difficult.
Another minor piece comes into play. The human-move model and the searched alternatives call this move difficult, and the engine puts it first. Quiet options can be the hardest to spot.
An unexpected way to get a minor piece out. Not a move the human-move model expects, and yet the engine's test says strong. Unusual ideas deserve a look.
A minor piece leaves home to join the plans. Here instinct and search agree, since the human-move model's favorite pick is also the move at the top of the engine's list.
One more minor piece enters the game. Natural in the human-move model's eyes and strong in the engine's test, though the engine's own choice is a different one.
The rook finds its way onto an open file. A well-hidden move that the engine ranks first and the human-move model rarely sees coming.
An unexpected route to the open file for the rook. The human-move model gives this move a low chance of being played, while the engine's comparison finds it strong.
The rook takes its place on an open file. Instinct and search land on the same option this time, since the human-move model expects it and nothing in the engine's comparison tops it.
An open file for the rook to work with. As ideas go, it's the natural one for the human-move model and a strong one for the engine, which would pick something else.
The rook takes up a semi-open file to work along. Top of the engine's option list, and the human-move model says few would find it. Worth remembering.
An unexpected route to a semi-open file for the rook. Seldom a human-move model candidate, and the engine's test passes it as strong.
The rook lands where enemy pawns stand but none of its own. If we line up every option, the human-move model's favorite is also the engine's, which is a nice thing to discover.
A semi-open file gives the rook something to press against. Natural as the human-move model scores it and strong as the engine tests it, with the engine's favorite being another move.
A passed pawn appears, one that no enemy pawn can block or capture on its file or beside it. Difficult to spot, as the human-move model scores it, and the best idea the engine found. Good exploring.
An unexpected idea that creates a passed pawn. Few players would try it, by the human-move model's estimate, yet it passes the engine's test as strong.
